newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's parliament passes single vote election law.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's parliament passes single vote election law.

text.p: Jordan's lower house of parliament approved on Sunday a law limiting voters to one vote each in November parliamentary elections despite vocal opposition from Islamist deputies.
Political analysts said the new law was aimed at weakening the representation of Islamists in parliament by preventing them from gaining many votes in large constituencies.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti described the ruling, which enshrines into law a temporary edict issued in 1993 before Jordan's first multi-party elections, as "the basis of any advanced parliamentary democracy in the world".
The law was approved by 51 of parliament's 80 deputies, the official Petra news agency said.
But Jordan's largest political party the Islamic Action Front (IAF) voted against the law which it said was a betrayal of voters.
Before 1993 voters had as many votes as there were seats in a constituency -- up to nine each in constituencies like Irbid province in the north of the country and Karak in the south.
Officials say the well-organised IAF, a political arm of the Moslem Brotherhood, capitalised on the multi-vote system to mobilise support in the larger constituencies.
Islamist sympathisers won nearly half of the 80 seats in the lower assembly in the 1989 non-party elections. But the IAF won only 17 seats in 1993 elections under the single vote.
Leading IAF deputy Abdallah Akaileh said the one-vote law was a direct attempt to undermine his party's influence and weaken the democratic process.
"The present electoral system doesn't reflect the political will of the people," he told Reuters. "It diminishes the will of the people by allowing them only to give a view on one deputy."
"It dwarfs parliamentary representation... by transforming a deputy into a representative of a (town) quarter or a tribe."
The IAF opposed Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel and the shift in its close ties to Iraq. It has also criticised tough domestic economic reforms.

Kabariti said opponents of the election law were portraying it as universally opposed by the voters. But he said the government was convinced "of the necessity to modernise, develop and keep abreast with changes."
"We are not convinced by people who accuse the government of repressing its people through proper democracy," Petra said Kabariti told parliament.

He said Sunday's law would stand until Jordan launched an overall review of the electoral system, including making constituencies more representative, quotas for women, and qualifications of candidates for parliament.
This year's elections, scheduled for November, will be the third since King Hussein set in motion a democratisation process in 1989 after nearly 40 years of absolute rule.
